We have carbon NMR data: many aromatic carbons (around 125-142 ppm) plus a carbon at 166.40 (likely carbonyl, maybe ester or amide) and a carbon at 52.24 (likely O-CH3 or CH2). The list: 166.40, 142.60, 133.69, 133.25, 132.62, 130.15 (twice), 129.32, 128.37, 128.16, 127.72, 127.15 (twice), 126.45, 125.88, 125.73, 125.50, 52.24. That's 17 signals. Could be a phenyl ring (6 carbons) plus maybe another aromatic ring (maybe biphenyl). 166 suggests carbonyl attached to aromatic (e.g., benzoic acid derivative). 52 suggests OCH3 (methoxy). So maybe methyl benzoate (C6H5COOCH3) would have carbonyl ~166, aromatic ~128-133 (6 signals), OCH3 ~52. That would be 8 carbons total, but we have 17 signals, many duplicates maybe due to symmetry? Actually methyl benzoate has 8 carbons, but we see 17 signals, so likely a larger aromatic system, maybe a naphthalene derivative? Naphthalene has 10 aromatic carbons, but we have many signals ~125-133 (maybe 10). Plus carbonyl and OCH3 gives 12. Still more than 17? Wait we have 17 signals total. Could be a phenyl ring plus a second phenyl ring (biphenyl) plus carbonyl and OCH3: that would be 12 aromatic carbons (two phenyl rings) + carbonyl + OCH3 = 14. Still less than 17. Maybe there are substituents causing more distinct carbons.

Let's get proton NMR to help.
